newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Refiners seek Rotterdam tanker dues cut by end May.
newsitem.headline: Refiners seek Rotterdam tanker dues cut by end May.

text.p: Leading oil refiners expect to hear by the end of May if their bid to reduce harbour dues levied on crude oil tankers by the Port of Rotterdam has been successful.
Oil refiners' representative association, the Oil Contact Committee (OCC), has petitioned the Municipality of Rotterdam to reduce the charges. A hearing will be held at the end of this month.
The refiners believe Rotterdam's harbour tariffs discriminate against the oil industry when compared with other sectors such as the container trade.
OCC chairman Cees Bakker said the association will take the matter to the courts if the action is not successful and the municipal council rejects their claim.

Bakker said the action specifically concerns crude oil tankers which are charged harbour dues of guilders 3.01 per gross tonne, whereas dry bulk carriers are charged guilders l.78 and container vessels guilders O.88.
The refiners are aiming to seek some reimbursement of the fees if the OCC is successful, he added.
Rotterdam is Europe's largest oil port.
"There is a vague claim by the port that it has had to invest more for the oil industry, but we believe it has not invested any more than it does for other shipping sectors," he said.
"Harbour dues represent 10 percent of our refining costs," he added.
OCC has approached independent tanker owners' association Intertanko in an effort to encourage its members to lobby the Dutch port over the level of dues.
An Intertanko spokesman acknowledged that the tariffs imposed on crude oil tankers are the highest at the port, but said the action was being taken by the refineries, not ship owners.

Intertanko does not generally tackle local port tariff issues, he said, although the organisation has brought the issue to the attention of its members. The spokesman added that shipowners feel they have little bargaining power.
A spokesman from the Port of Rotterdam said the port is studying the refiners' protest. But he said the OCC cannot proceed with legal action unless it gets the shipowners' backing.
However, OCC's Bakker said the refiners believe they can object in their own right.
The OCC takes the view that the refiners pay the harbour dues eventually as they are included in the costs of transportation, said Bakker.
